AMENDED RESOLUTION NO. 34 OF 2026

A RESOLUTION SETTING FORTH REVIEW CRITERIA AND
PROCEDURES DURING THE CURRENT SUSPENSION OF THE
FLOCK CAMERAS; AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES

WHEREAS, on the evening of August 6, 2026, Mayor Kincade announced an immediate
suspension of the Cabot Police Department’s Flock camera program pending further
comprehensive review. The cameras were unplugged and physically covered the next morning
also pending said review; and

WHEREAS, The Cabot City Council wishes to establish certain criteria and procedures for
the Flock camera program review as set forth herein; and

WHEREAS, the City Council herein establishes the criteria and procedures for the Flock
camera program review.

NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED BY THE CITY COUNCIL OF CABOT,
ARKANSAS THAT:

SECTION 1: The Mayor has suspended the Cabot Police Department’s Flock
camera program pending further comprehensive review. This review should be done
according to the following criteria and procedures:

a. The review will be conducted by the Cabot Chief of Police and a group of
people to be selected by the Chief.

b. The review will be comprehensive and will include, without limitation, the
ways in which Flock cameras have been utilized by the Cabot Police
Department and the security/privacy measures and policies in place governing
the use of said cameras.

c. The review, if not already commenced, will begin immediately upon passage
of this Resolution and may take up to thirty days therefrom.

d. The findings of the review shall be presented to the City Council at a City
Council meeting within sixty days of the passage of this Resolution. At that
meeting, the City Council may take whatever action it deems appropriate
regarding the suspension, reinstatement, or termination of the Cabot Police
Department’s Flock camera program.

SECTION 2: A public hearing on this matter shall be conducted on October 19,

2026 at 6:30 pm.

SECTION 3: This resolution shall be in full force and effect from and after its

passage.

License Plate Reader(s) Policy # 305.1

This policy is for internal use only and does not enlarge an employee’s civil liability in any way. The
policy should not be construed as creating a higher duty of care, in an evidentiary sense, with
respect to third party civil claims against employees. A violation of this policy, if proven, can only
form the basis of a complaint by this department for non-judicial administrative action in
accordance with the laws governing employee discipline.

Applicable Arkansas Statutes:

ALEAP Accreditation Standards:

Date Implemented: Review Schedule: Issuing Authority:
September 13, 2022 Biennial Chief Scott Steely

I. PURPOSE: The purpose of this policy is to provide employees of the Cabot Police
Department with guidelines for application and use of license plate readers (LPR),
management of LPR data.

II. POLICY: Itis the policy of the Cabot Police Department to use license plate readers to enhance law
enforcement’s ability to detect violations of law, recover stolen property, locate missing persons, apprehend
fugitives, assist in investigations, and other tasks accordance with procedures and guidelines set forth in this
policy. Additionally, data captured from LPR’s will be used properly as defined herein.

Il. DEFINITIONS:
Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR): A device that uses infrared and/or high-
resolution digital cameras and other optical character recognition technology to scan the
license plate of moving and/or stationary motor vehicles and compare the scanned
information to one or more databases to identify license plates and subsequent vehicles or
registered owners that may be associated with unlawful activity.

LPR SYSTEM: The LPR and all associated equipment and databases.

HOT LIST: Any database that contains lists of license plate numbers that are of interest
to the police personnel, such as those associated with vehicles and/or license plates that
have been stolen, wanted for specific crimes, or those that are associated with, or may
assist with the identification of, suspects involved in criminal activity. This will also
include data held by the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), Office of Motor
Vehicles, the Arkansas Crime Information Center (ACIC) including without limitation

Iv.

the Arkansas Crime Information Center’s Missing Persons Database, the National Crime
Information Center, and the Federal Bureau of Investigating Kidnapping and Missing
Persons database.

LPR DATA: Data obtained by an LPR from license plates that were read by the device,
including potential images of the plate, the vehicle on which it is displayed, the date and
time, and information regarding the location of the LPR is installed and any other data
captured by or derived from any automatic license plate reader system, and, which may
be stored on the Department’s computer system or maintained and stored in the LPR’s
secured data storage online.

HOT: LPR data read that matched to a license plate that has been previously uploaded on
a Departmental “Hot List” or previously assigned in a category provided by the LPR data
software and registered with the National Crime Information Center.

PROCEDURES:
A. Only authorized LPR systems owned, leased or provided by the Department will be used.

B. LPR users will be assigned by the Chief of Police or his/her designee.

C. LPR’s will be used only by members who have been trained in the operation and use
of the LPR system.

D. Data added to the Department HOT LIST will only be done by those assigned
by the Chief of Police or his/her designee.

E. A LPR HOT LIST hit shall not be used as the sole reason for a traffic stop or
enforcement contact. Contact with the vehicle and its occupants will only be
made after the license plate in the hot list hit is physically located and confirmed
by visual and ACIC/NCIC confirmation.

LPR OPERATION:
A. LPR’s may be used during.

Regular patrol duties,

Special operations or details such as high crime area patrols,

STEP activities,

Directed patrols,

Assisting in criminal investigations, and

Other activities as approved by the Chief of Police, or his/her designee.

me ae rE
VII.

B. Upon receiving a “hit notification”, the mobile LPR operator will visually verify the
displayed information matches the subject license plate (i.e. correct letters, numbers,
state of issue, and any other verifiable information.)

C. Upon verifying the alert is valid, the mobile LPR operator will take appropriate action
based upon the type of “hit notification” in accordance with training, department
policy, NCIC/ACIC Regulation and law.

D. LPR data received from LPR servers will be accessed for criminal justice reasons
only, by those users authorized by the Chief of Police, or his/her designee and who
have been issued an individual username and password for access.

E. Usernames and Passwords shall not be shared between users. Users accessing the
LPR data must do so from their own username and password provided.

LPR DATA:

A. Any LPR data that involves a hot list hit and the hit is confirmed by locating the
license plate that received the hit will be documented in a report or a CAD entry.

B. Any investigation from a hot list hit, from which an enforcement action, an
investigation, or a prosecution resulted, will be documented in a report, and added to
any case file prepared for prosecution.

C. Captured plate data that indicates evidence of an offense may be shared with other
law enforcement agencies. Captured plate data may not be otherwise shared, sold,
traded, or exchanged.

D. Captured plate data shall not be preserved by the Cabot Police Department for more
than 150 days from date of capture. No later than 150 days from capture, the
captured plate data will be deleted or otherwise destroyed as appropriate.
Notwithstanding the 150-day limit, captured plate data may be retained longer as part
of an ongoing investigation and shall be destroyed at the conclusion of either: an
investigation that does not result in any criminal charges being filed; or any criminal
action undertaken in the matter involving the captured plate data.

E. The Cabot Police Department shall update the captured plate data collected every 24
hours if updates are available.

REPORTS

A. Cabot Police Department command level commander or designee will compile
Vil.

IX.

statistical data every six (6) months into a report and the report presented to the Chief
of Police. Each report shall be preserved for eighteen (18) months.

The report will be in such a format sufficient to allow the general public to review it
upon request.

The report will include the following data:

1. The number of license plates scanned; and

2. The names of the lists against which the captured plate data were checked (ex.
NCIC/ACIC);

3. The number of confirmed matches;

4. The number of matches upon further investigation that did not correlate to an
alert;

5. The number of matches that resulted in arrest and prosecution.

PRIVACY

Captured plate data or data obtained from the Office of Motor Vehicle may be disclosed

only:

1. To the person to whom the vehicle is registered; or

2. After written consent of the person to whom the vehicle is registered; or

3. Ifthe disclosure is permitted under the Driver’s Privacy Protection Act of 1994,
18 U.S.C. 2721 et seq., as it existed on January 1, 2013.

Practice and usage data compiled and preserved for use in a trial, hearing, or other
proceeding before an authoritative body of the state or political subdivision of the state
pursuant to 12-12-1806 are a public record for purposes of the Arkansas Freedom of
Information Act.

Upon the presentation to an appropriate governmental entity of a valid, outstanding
protection order protecting the driver of a vehicle jointly registered with or registered
solely in the name of the individual against whom the order was issued, captured plate
data shall not be disclosed except as the result of a match under A.C.A. 12-12-1803.

POLICY

This policy is subject to inspection and copying by a member of the general public upon
request.

12-12-1802. Definitions.

As used in this subchapter:
(1) “Alert” means data held by the Office of Motor Vehicle, the Arkansas Crime Information
Center including without limitation the Arkansas Crime Information Center's Missing Persons

Information Clearinghouse, the National Crime Information Center, and the Federal Bureau of
Investigation Kidnappings and Missing Persons database;

(2) “Automatic license plate reader system” means a system of one (1) or more mobile or
fixed automated high-speed cameras used in combination with computer algorithms to
convert images of license plates into computer-readable data;

(3)

(A) “Captured plate data” means the global positioning device coordinates, date and time,
photograph, license plate number, and any other data captured by or derived from any
automatic license plate reader system.

(B) Captured plate data shall not include any personal data;

(4) “Governmental entity” means a lawfully created branch, department, or agency of the
federal, state, or local government;

(5) “Private landowner, private leaseholder, or commercial business” means a landowner,
leaseholder, or commercial business that is not a governmental entity; and

(6) “Secured area” means an area, enclosed by clear boundaries, to which access is limited
and not open to the public, and entry is obtainable only through specific access-control

points.

History

Acts 2013, No. 1491, § 1; 2025, No. 668, § 1.

12-12-1803. Restrictions on use.

(a) Except as provided in subsection (b) of this section, it is unlawful for an individual,
partnership, corporation, limited liability company, association, or the State of Arkansas, its

agencies, and political subdivisions to use an automatic license plate reader system.

(b) An automatic license plate reader system may be used:

(1) By a state, county, or municipal law enforcement agency for the comparison of captured
plate data with data held by the Office of Motor Vehicle, the Arkansas Crime Information
Center, the National Crime Information Center, a database created by law enforcement for the
purposes of an ongoing investigation, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation for any lawful
purpose;

(2) By parking enforcement entities for regulating the use of parking facilities;

(3) For the purpose of controlling access to secured areas;

(4) By a private landowner, private leaseholder, or commercial business for the purpose of
promoting public safety, deterring crime, and monitoring access to private property owned or
leased by the private landowner, private leaseholder, or commercial business, including
ingress and egress to private property on a private road owned by the private landowner,
private leaseholder, or commercial business; or

(5)

(A) By the Arkansas Highway Police Division of the Arkansas Department of Transportation
for the electronic verification of registration, logs, and other compliance data to provide more

efficient movement of commercial vehicles on a state highway.

(B) An automatic license plate reader system used under subdivision (b)(5)(A) of this section

shall be installed at an entrance ramp at a weigh station facility for the review of a
commercial motor vehicle entering the weigh station facility.

History

12-12-1804. Protections.

(a) Except as provided under subsection (b) of this section, captured plate data obtained for the purposes described
under § 12-12-1803(b) shall not be preserved for more than:

(1) Sixty (60) days by a private landowner, private leaseholder, or commercial business; or

(2) One hundred fifty (150) days by all other eligible entities.

(b) Captured plate data obtained by an entity under § 12-12-1803(b)(1) may be retained as part of an ongoing
investigation and shall be destroyed at the conclusion of either:

(1) An investigation that does not result in any criminal charges being filed; or

(2) Any criminal action undertaken in the matter involving the captured plate data.

(c) A governmental entity that uses an automatic license plate reader system under § 12-12-1803(b)(1) shall update
the captured plate data collected under this subchapter every twenty-four (24) hours if updates are available.

(d)

(1) Except as provided under subdivision (d)(2) of this section, a governmental entity authorized to use an automatic
license plate reader system under § 12-12-1803(b) shall not sell, trade, or exchange captured plate data for any
purpose.

(2) Captured plate data obtained by a law enforcement agency under § 12-12-1803(b)(1) that indicates evidence of
an offense may be shared with other law enforcement agencies.

(3) A governmental entity may only compel the release of captured plate data from a user under § 12-12-1803(b)(2),
§ 12-12-1803(b)(3), § 12-12-1803(b)(4), or § 25-16-705(a) through a valid subpoena.

(e)

(1) Except as provided under subdivision (e)(2) of this section, a private landowner, private leaseholder, or commercial
business authorized to use an automatic license plate reader system under § 12-12-1803(b) shall not sell, trade, or
exchange captured plate data for any commercial purpose.

(2)

(A) Captured plate data obtained by a private landowner, private leaseholder, or commercial business under § 12-12-
1803(b)(4) may be shared with a third-party processor providing asset protection analytical services on the captured
plate data as part of a contractual agreement with the private landowner, private leaseholder, or commercial business.
(B) The terms of the contractual agreement shall expressly prohibit a third-party processor from using the captured
plate data for any other purpose and impose a data retention period not to exceed sixty (60) days from receipt of the
captured plate data.

(a) An entity that uses an automatic license plate reader system under § 12-12-1803(b)(1),
§ 12-12-1803(b)(2), § 12-12-1803(b)(3), or § 12-12-1803(b)(5) shall:

(2) Preserve the compiled data for eighteen (18) months; and

(3)

(A) Promulgate rules and policies concerning the manner and method of obtaining, retaining,
and destroying captured plate data, including without limitation specific rules and policies
concerning retention of material in excess of one hundred fifty (150) days under § 12-12-
1804(b), and make those rules and policies available for public inspection.

(B) Failure to comply with subdivision (a)(3)(A) of this section shall be grounds for a court of
competent jurisdiction to exclude any evidence obtained under this subchapter.

(b) The preserved data shall include:

(1) The number of license plates scanned;

(2) The names of the lists against which captured plate data were checked; and

(3) For each check of captured plate data against a list:

(A) The number of confirmed matches;

(B) The number of matches that upon further investigation did not correlate to an alert; and
(C) The number of matches that resulted in arrest and prosecution.

(c) A private landowner, private leaseholder, or commercial business that uses an automatic
license plate reader system under § 12-12-1803(b)(4) shall:

(1) Compile statistical data every six (6) months that includes the:

(B) Number of confirmed matches; and

12-12-1806. Use of data and data-derived evidence.

Captured plate data and evidence derived from it shall not be received in evidence in any trial, hearing, or other
proceeding before any court, grand jury, department, officer, agency, regulatory body, legislative committee, or other
authority of the state or a political subdivision of the state if the disclosure of that information would be in violation of
this subchapter.

PUBLIC INFORMATION RELEASE
ATTEMPTED KIDNAPPING SOLVED IN 12 HOURS

August 25, 2022, around 2:30am the Cabot Police Officers were dispatched to an attempted
kidnapping at a local truck stop. Officers arrived and met with the victim. The victim advised a
white male entered her truck, held a knife to her, and attempted to kidnap her. She resisted by
punching him in the face and then ran inside the business. The suspect went back to his vehicle
and drove away the area.

Patrol officers checked our ALPR cameras and notified our detectives what was located.

From the store security video, detectives were able to identify the vehicle as a white Ford Taurus
between the years of 2000-2007. A check of the ALPR camera system showed 16 vehicles that met
that description had been in the Cabot city limits in the past two weeks. Two of the vehicles had
distinctive pinstriping down both sides. The pinstriping of one of those vehicles matched the
pinstriping visible in the video from the store where the attempted kidnapping took place. That
vehicle was a 2006 white Ford Taurus. That vehicle was photographed by the ALPR system on
8/24/2022 at 1418 hours northbound on S. 2nd St. in Cabot. The license plate on that vehicle was
registered to Gary Ollison. Detectives viewed Gary Ollison's photo and positively identified Gary
Ollison as the male suspect in the video from the store who attempted to kidnap our victim.

Suspect Ollison was a Level 3 Sex Offender registered in a neighboring county's jurisdiction.
Detectives continued this investigation, including search warrants, that led them to locate the
suspect at his job and take him into custody. The suspect was arrested and charged within 12 hours
from the time he tried to kidnap the young lady.

Ollison was charged and convicted of Aggravated Assault, Criminal Attempted Kidnapping, and
Breaking or Entering.

The ALPR technology allowed the Cabot Police Department to narrow the focus of the
investigation quickly, identify the potential suspect vehicle, and act as part of the investigative
evidence to secure warrants and the arrest of the suspect.

PUBLIC INFORMATION RELEASE
MURDER SUSPECT ARRESTED

February 13th, 2026, Cabot Police Department received an ALPR alert for a possible stolen vehicle
traveling on S. Pine Street in Cabot, Arkansas. The Patrol Sergeant asked dispatchers to confirm
the license plate. The vehicle was confirmed to have been stolen from Faulkner County. Officers
located the vehicle and performed a felony traffic stop. The on-duty Sergeant arrived quickly and
assisted. The suspect was taken into custody without incident. The vehicle was confirmed stolen
out of Conway, Arkansas. Other Officers arrived during this time to assist with the situation. A tow
truck was called for the vehicle and the Patrol Lieutenant assisted with the vehicle inventory. While
inventorying the trunk of the vehicle the Lieutenant located a shirt with an abnormal amount of
blood on it and the blood appeared to be wet. Officers also located blood drops in the trunk area.

The Cabot Police Department Criminal Investigation Division was notified. The vehicle was towed
to the Cabot Police Department evidence bay where a further investigation took place. The suspect
was transported to the Cabot Police Department and booked for felony Theft by Receiving. During
the investigation, it was determined that this suspect was allegedly involved in a homicide in White
County Arkansas that took place just prior to this traffic stop. The driver of the vehicle who the
Cabot Police Department took into custody, Britini Reveley, was arrested and preliminary charged
with Capital Murder, Residential Burglary and Tampering with Physical Evidence in the death of
Brian Radak by the White County Sheriff’s Department.

SEX OFFENDER INVESTIGATION FEBRUARY 2026

In February of 2026 officers had an interaction with a level 3 sex offender who showed to be
registered in White County, AR. Detectives began an investigation believing he was actually out
of compliance and living in Cabot. Detectives used the ALRP cameras and found from February
2nd through February 25th the vehicle associated with the sex offender registered 63 times on the
Cabot PD ALPRs. This led to an address in Cabot where it was found he was actually living, he
had an unreported job of Door Dashing food, and was actually living within 2,000 feet of a Cabot
School. He was arrested.

On March 3rd, shortly after this arrest, detectives used ALPR cameras to assist with a sex offender
compliance check with this same individual. Another investigation occurred and found the same
level 3 sex offender was staying in Cabot again within 2000 feet of a Cabot school. He was
arrested again.

Officers continued investigating this individual and it was later discovered he had CSAM (child
sexual assault material) what we refer to as child pornography digital images on his cell
phone. Cabot detectives arrested him.

In this example the ALPR images provided evidence of a sex offender illegally living in our city
near a school. This use helped build a case that eventually led to the discovery of child
pornography and a sex offender returning to jail.

PUBLIC INFORMATION RELEASE
FELONY HIT AND RUN TO BICYCLE RIDER

On July 30th, 2026, Cabot Police Department officers were dispatched to the W. Main overpass.
We were informed an individual riding a bicycle had been struck by a vehicle. Witnesses reported
finding the cyclist unresponsive with blood coming from his nose and mouth. Officers later
learned he sustained two broken legs, a large laceration on his leg, bleeding on the brain, cracked
and shattered teeth, and multiple facial fractures. The vehicle that struck the cyclist did not stop,
did not get help, it fled the scene. A bystander reported they believed the suspect vehicle to be a
white Honda Odyssey. Officers on scene were able to later determine the suspect vehicle was
actually a silver SUV.

The following morning, Detectives used all this information and began investigating. A search of
the Cabot Police Department ALPRs (based on vehicle description, time of day, and direction of
travel) revealed a probable match for the suspect vehicle. Upon arriving at the address of the
suspect vehicle, detectives found a vehicle with significant damage to the front and its front bumper
missing. Detectives also found what appeared to be hair embedded in pillar next to the windshield.
Based on the digital ALPR evidence, the physical evidence located, and an interview with a
potential suspect, detectives were able to make an arrest.

Initial bystander observation of the suspect vehicle was not correct. The digital evidence revealed
from searching the ALPRs allowed the Cabot Police Department to identify the correct vehicle
and continue the investigation.

New from the IACP: IACP Statement on ALPR Use and Launch of
ALPR Resource Page

The International Association of Chiefs of Police (ACP) strongly supports the lawful, ethical, transparent, and accountable use of
Automated License Plate Recognition (ALPR) technology when it advances legitimate public safety objectives, including preventing and
solving crime, protecting community members and officers, locating missing, endangered, and vulnerable persons, and recovering stolen
property.

©
IACP

When properly used, ALPR can locate vehicles connected to violent crimes and other serious offenses, generate investigative leads,
improve officer safety, and direct limited public safety resources more effectively. These capabilities strengthen emergency response and
criminal investigations.

IACP’s support for ALPR technology is grounded in an equally strong commitment to constitutional policing, individual privacy, civil rights,
civil liberties, and public trust. Because ALPR systems may create records containing a license plate image, a contextual vehicle image, and
the date, time, and location, agencies must carefully manage how this data is collected, accessed, retained, analyzed, and shared. Strong
safeguards protect individual rights and sustain public confidence, essential to effective policing.

Responsible ALPR programs should include these core safeguards:
e Use ALPR technology and data only for a documented, lawful public safety purpose.
e Limit access to trained, authorized personnel and prohibit personal, political, retaliatory, discriminatory, commercial, or other
unauthorized use.
e Maintain a comprehensive written policy covering authorized uses, deployment, hot lists, training, accuracy, access, security,
sharing, retention, complaints, audits, and consequences for misuse.
e Treat each ALPR alert as an investigative lead, not conclusive evidence. Confirm the plate, jurisdiction, record status, and connection
to the driver before taking enforcement action.
e Maintain tamper-resistant audit records and conduct regular audits, supervisory reviews, and periodic evaluations towerify
authorized use, data accuracy, retention compliance, and public safety value.
e Investigate suspected misuse promptly. Apply appropriate corrective or disciplinary action, including administrative, civil, or criminal
accountability, when warranted, and use audit findings to improve policies, training, security, and system controls.
© Protect ALPR data with appropriate cybersecurity, authentication, access controls, and data-integrity measures. Retain data only as
long as it serves an authorized purpose, then purge it promptly.
e Share ALPR information only with authorized entities for legitimate purposes under written agreements that preserve access limits,
security, auditing, retention requirements, and restrictions on secondary use. Document each disclosure.
In addition, to help address questions and concerns regarding ALPR technology, the IACP has convened a diverse working group of law
enforcement leaders, practitioners, subject matter experts, and key stakeholders to develop guidance, resources, and leading practices
that support the responsible use of ALPR systems.

As part of this ongoing effort, the IACP has launched a new ALPR Resource Page that serves as a central hub for information, tools, and
educational materials on the responsible use of ALPR technology. The page will be regularly updated with new resources, guidance, and
leading practices developed through the working group's efforts, providing agencies with practical tools to navigate the evolving policy and
operational landscape surrounding ALPR.

Arkansas Sheriffs' Association Position on Automated

The Arkansas Sheriffs' Association supports the
responsible use ofAutomated License Plate

Reader (ALPR) technology as an important tool for
enhancing public safety and assisting law enforcement
agencies in protecting the communities they serve.
Sheriffs across Arkansas face increasingly complex
public safety challenges that require the effective use of
technology. When implemented appropriately, ALPR
systems can assist in locating missing and endangered
persons, identifying stolen vehicles, developing
investigative leads, apprehending criminal offenders, and
improving officer safety. These technologies provide
valuable information that can help law enforcement
agencies respond more quickly and efficiently to threats
affecting Arkansas citizens.

The Association recognizes that the use of ALPR
technology must be balanced with a commitment to
constitutional protections, individual privacy, and the
preservation of public trust. As with any law enforcement
tool, accountability, transparency, and proper oversight
are essential to ensuring its appropriate use.

The Arkansas Sheriffs' Association encourages agencies
utilizing ALPR technology to adopt policies and practices
that include:

e Clearly defined and lawful public safety purposes for
the use of ALPR systems.

e Written policies governing deployment, access,
training, retention, auditing, and information sharing.

e Access is limited to authorized personnel who have
received appropriate training.

e Regular review and auditing of systems is used to
ensure compliance with agency policy and applicable
law.
e Appropriate safeguards to protect collected data from
unauthorized access, misuse, or disclosure.

e Verification of ALPR alerts before enforcement action
is taken, recognizing that alerts serve as investigative
information rather than definitive proof.

e Prompt investigation of misuse and appropriate
corrective action when violations occur.

The Arkansas Sheriffs' Association believes ALPR
technology can be a valuable public safety asset when
used responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with
the law Sheriffs remain committed to protecting both the
safety and the rights of Arkansas citizens while utilizing
modern tools that support effective policing and criminal
investigations. As technology continues to evolve, the
Association will support best practices, professional
training, and policies that promote both public safety and
public confidence in law enforcement. Arkansas Sheriffs
Association will be presenting a Bill to add or increase
criminal penalties for misuse of ALPRs during the 2027
General Assembly

RESOLUTION by the Lonoke County Republican Committee on

The installation and use of FLOCK cameras

The undersigned hereby certify that the following resolution was adopted at the
2026 September meeting of the LCRC.

Resolve. The members of the LCRC express our concern regarding the FLOCK
camera system that is being installed in our county and the collection, storage,
and dissemination of personal data. We believe, where in some cases the
information can lead to the apprehension of criminals, the solving of crimes and
even the saving of lives, the intrusion in our personal lives and the storing of our
travels, habits, and other private activities although are not illegal, can be used by
unscrupulous persons if they get access to this information. We also know that
this information has been used to track and harass innocent people by those who
have access to it and use it illegally.

Resolve. A copy of this resolution will be provided to the Mayor, each member of
the City Council and head of the Police department of each city in Lonoke County.
That a copy will be provided to the County Judge and each member of the
Quorum Court. That a copy be provided to the County Sheriff.

Resolve, That this resolution be presented to the District 1 Republican Committee
for their consideration and to the State Republican Committee for their
consideration.

Jennifer Hopper

Good morning,

Today | want to share several updates on how Flock is further addressing three
areas that are critical to the company: strengthening privacy, accountability, and
security.

Privacy

When we started Flock 9 years ago, we set the default ALPR retention period to
30 days, unless state or local policy decided on a shorter or longer period. We
believed this struck a careful balance between safety and privacy.

Today, we are updating our recommendation and default to a 7 day retention,
and introducing “Evidence Mode.” Our analysis shows that over 90% of
searches without a full plate are done within a week. Evidence Mode, which will
roll out in the coming weeks, addresses the exceptional cases that take longer:
detectives can preserve specific ALPR data as evidence for an active
investigation in cold storage, consistent with existing laws and policies.

Existing customers will keep their current, democratically approved retention
periods. Customers who adopt the 7-day recommendation will receive Evidence
Mode at no cost. Every community will continue to choose the retention period
that fits its public safety strategy.

We are also introducing Offense filtering for sharing. Now, cities can choose
which type of offenses are permissible for other agencies to access their
cameras. For example, City A could allow City B to search its cameras only for a
stolen vehicle, missing person, or violent crime while blocking searches related
to immigration enforcement. This gives communities more control over data
sharing while preserving collaboration where policies align.

Accountability

Abuse of Flock technology, at any level, is unacceptable. We have strengthened
safeguards over the past nine years, from basic audit logs to proactive
monitoring. 16 weeks ago, we introduced Audit Assistance, which detects
abnormal activity and flags it for Administrator review. In recent weeks, those
reviews have been associated with arrests of several law enforcement officers
who allegedly abused the system. More than one-third of our customers have
voluntarily adopted Audit Assistance.

We will now require all law enforcement customers to adopt this feature by the
end of this year. In addition, we will institute proactive lockout. When a user’s
activity meets defined criteria for abnormal behavior, Flock will automatically
suspend access pending administrator review. The goal is to intervene before
misuse becomes recurring or widespread.

In July 2025, we introduced an optional case code requirement for searches.
Results from participating agencies have been promising, so we will

now require case codes for all law enforcement searches by the end of year.
Agencies may bypass the requirement in emergencies, but every exigent search
will be flagged for administrator review.

Data Ownership

From the beginning, we have been clear that our customers own the data
captured by their ALPR cameras. This has always been the case, but some of
our contractual language has confused the public on this crucial point. To make
that commitment easier to understand, next week we will publish an easy to
read / plain English explanation of our contract on our website, organized
section by section. The principle is simple: customers own the data, decide who
can access it, and choose who they share with.

Data Security

Flock is committed to the strongest security program in the industry. This year
we retained Bishop Fox, a leading independent security firm, to conduct a
thorough review of our products and capabilities. We will publish its summary of
findings and our remediations in September.

We're also launching a Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure program (CVD).
Flock’s CVD gives security researchers a safe, credited path to report and
disclose their work while receiving recognition. Researchers can disclose issues
at vulnerability.disclosure@flocksafety.com.

At the beginning of this month, we also made multi-factor authentication (MFA)
mandatory for anyone logging into Flock, increasing our security standards for
all customers.

Security is an ongoing responsibility. We will continue testing, improving, and
updating our controls.

Data Accuracy

Arecent story described a wrongful traffic stop involving an auto journalist. The
central point is simple: an alert is a lead, not a conclusion, which should be
confirmed by an officer.

Let me explain a little about how this technology works. Basic optical character
recognition can see the numbers and characters on a license plate and report
whatever it sees. Flock goes further, using machine learning models trained on
plate designs from all 50 states, including stacked and undersized characters,
and are retrained weekly as plate designs change. Every read carries a
confidence score, and low-confidence reads are flagged as such, never
presented as certainties and never sent as alerts to officers.

Recognition is only the first step. Before an alert goes out, the Flock system
matches both the plate and the issuing state against the hotlist record. The
system then filters out low-confidence reads before sending alerts to officers.

The final safeguard is human. Before acting, an officer visually confirms the
plate and confirms the stop complies with law and agency policy. No stop should
ever rest on an unverified alert standing alone.

This combined system of safeguards results in fewer than 9 human reported
errors for every 1 million alerts.

Transparency

More than 1,500 agencies have published a Flock Transparency Portal. If your
agency has not published one, please, turn it on. The portal gives your
community a direct view of your policy, retention period, sharing partners, and
search activity, in your agency’s own words.

Why Now?

Nine years ago, we set out to build a company that would make communities
safer. Today, Flock technology assists your officers in more than one million
crimes solved annually. In July alone, with your help, we detected over 1,000
missing people and over 20,000 stolen cars.

These changes reflect years of work and deliberation. They are not the end of
that work, but simply the continuation of our commitment to both safety and
privacy. We are not perfect, so we will keep listening, improving, and building a
better standard for public safety technology together. You'll receive additional
updates from us in the weeks and months ahead as these changes roll out.

Flock AWS Account Team
Summary

One of the questions customers ask is: "How do | know my data is actually deleted?"
This is a fair question — especially for organizations handling sensitive data subject to
compliance requirements like CJIS. This white paper explains how AWS ensures data is
permanently removed from Amazon S3 buckets, and how Flock’s use of these services
in their AWS environment — S3 Lifecycle Policies, AWS CloudTrail, Amazon
CloudWatch, and Amazon OpenSearch — work together to provide verifiable proof that
deletion has occurred.

The short answer: AWS provides multiple layers of evidence — from API-level audit
logs to automated deletion policies to real-time monitoring — that together create an
airtight chain of custody that your data has been permanently removed.

How S3 Deletion Actually Works
What Happens When You Delete an Object

When an object is deleted from Amazon S3, the behavior depends on whether
versioning is enabled:

e Without versioning: The object is permanently deleted. It cannot be recovered.
AWS confirms the deletion by returning a "deleted" result in the API response.

e With versioning: A "delete marker" is placed on the object, making it invisible to
normal requests. The previous version still exists until you explicitly delete it or a
lifecycle policy removes it.

e Permanent deletion of a version: When you delete a specific object version (or
when a lifecycle policy expires it), that version is permanently removed from AWS
infrastructure. It cannot be recovered by anyone — including AWS.

Key Point: Deletion Is Irreversible

AWS documentation is explicit: "Deleting an object can't be undone." Once an object or
object version is permanently deleted, there is no mechanism — not even for AWS
engineers — to retrieve it. This is by design and is enforced at the infrastructure level.

S3 Lifecycle Policies: Automated, Guaranteed Deletion
What They Do

$3 Lifecycle Policies are configurable rules that automatically manage objects
throughout their life.

Page 1

1. The policy is declarative and auditable: Your lifecycle configuration is stored
as part of the bucket's settings. You can retrieve it at any time to confirm what
rules are in place.

2. $3 executes lifecycle rules automatically: Once configured, AWS guarantees
execution. Objects that meet the expiration criteria will be deleted — there is no
manual step that could be skipped.

3. CloudTrail logs the lifecycle actions: Every object expiration triggered by a
lifecycle policy generates a CloudTrail event, giving you a timestamped record of
what was deleted and when.

4. You can verify absence: After expiration, attempting to retrieve the object
returns a "404 Not Found" or "NoSuchKey" error — direct proof the object no
longer exists.

EXAMPLE-A typical compliance-oriented lifecycle policy might include:
e Permanently delete noncurrent versions after 30 days
e Remove expired delete markers after 1 day

AWS CloudTrail: Your Deletion Audit Trail
What CloudTrail Captures

AWS CloudTrail records every API call made in your AWS account. For S3 deletion, this
includes:
e DeleteObject — Records who deleted what object, from which bucket, at what
time, and from what IP address.
e DeleteObjects (batch) — Same as above, but for bulk deletions.
e Lifecycle-triggered expirations — In addition to Amazon CloudTrail, Amazon
S3 Server access logging provides detailed records for the requests that are
made to a bucket. When S3 automatically deletes objects based on lifecycle
rules, they are captured in Amazon S3 server access logs.
e PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration — Records when lifecycle policies are
created or modified, and by whom.

Why This Matters for Proving Deletion

AWS CloudTrail and S3 Server Access Logging gives you:

e Who performed or triggered the deletion
What was deleted (bucket name, object key, version ID)
When it happened (precise timestamp)
How it was initiated (console, CLI, SDK, or lifecycle automation)
Tamper-proof records: CloudTrail supports log file integrity validation. You can
cryptographically verify that log files have not been modified, deleted, or forged
after delivery. This means your deletion records are forensically sound.

Metrics That Prove Deletion Is Happening

CloudWatch provides S3 bucket-level metrics that give you visibility into deletion

e NumberOfObjects: Track the total object count in a bucket over time. A

Elijah Porter was charged with possession of a machinegun in violation
of 18 U.S.C. § 922(0). He challenges (1) the denial of his motion to suppress
vehicle-location data obtained from a license plate reader (“LPR”) and a
firearm obtained in a vehicle search and (2) the district court’s ruling that
18 U.S.C. § 922(0) is not unconstitutional. Because the use of an LPR did
not constitute a search, no warrant was required; the stop was supported by

I. Factual Background
A. Evidentiary Hearing
At the suppression hearing, the district court heard testimony from
Charles Hoggard, a former officer for the Gautier Police Department. Video
footage from Hoggard’s body camera was also presented.

1. Officer Hoggard’s Testimony

While on patrol in January 2024, Hoggard received an alert on his
phone that an LPR located at a specific intersection captured the license
plate of a vehicle that was associated with criminal activity. He contacted
dispatch and was told that the vehicle was “associated with” Elijah Porter,
who had a warrant for aggravated assault. Hoggard conducted a computer
check for the license plate, which revealed the vehicle was associated with
“James Stewart” or “E.L. Porter.” He located the vehicle and conducted a
traffic stop.

After identifying Porter as the driver, Hoggard detained him and pat-
ted him down. Hoggard observed a firearm protruding from under the
driver’s seat. He was able to see the slide and barrel of the firearm, and a
“Jittle silver switch on the back of it,” which he “believed to be the switch of

Automated License Plate Readers

Acronyms and Definitions’

Alert: A read matched to a license plate that has previously been identified as a vehicle license plate of interest, or which
has been manually registered for detection (may also be referred to as a hif).

Automated license plate recognition/automated license plate reader (ALPR): A device that passively records license plates
of vehicles.

Fixed ALPR system: ALPR cameras that are affixed to a structure, such as a pole, a traffic barrier, or a bridge.
FOUO: For official use only.

Hot list: License plate numbers of interest to police. Hot list information can come from multiple authorized sources
across different agencies and organizations.

Mobile ALPR system: ALPR cameras that are affixed to an authorized vehicle for mobile deployment, either permanently
(hardwired) or temporarily (e.g., magnet-mounted).

Portable ALPR system: ALPR cameras that are transportable and can be moved and deployed in a variety of venues.

Read: Digital images of license plates and/or vehicles and associated metadata (e.g., date, time, and geographic
coordinates associated with the vehicle image capture) that are captured by the ALPR system (may also be referred to as a
detection or scan).

User: Any individual who is authorized to access information and use the ALPR system. This could be professional staff
or a sworn officer.

Automated License Plate Readers

Il. PURPOSE

The purpose of this policy is to provide agency personnel with guidelines on the proper use of agency-operated
automated license plate recognition (ALPR) systems, also commonly known as automated license plate reader systems.

Il. POLICY

It is the policy of this agency that ALPR systems and their associated data be used to quickly identify vehicles of
interest to further efficient and effective police operations with consideration for public and officer safety and protection
of civil liberties.

Ill. Procedures

A. General

The use of ALPR systems and associated data is restricted to official purposes only.

2. ALPR systems and associated data are the property of this agency and are intended for use in conducting
official business.

3. Misuse of this equipment and associated databases or data may be subject to sanctions and/or disciplinary
actions.

4. This agency’s users should ensure that human verification takes place prior to any action taken as a result of
an ALPR hit, and for any data that is entered into the system.

B. Administration

This agency is responsible for the following:

1. Designating an employee(s) with administrative oversight for ALPR system deployment and operations.

2. Establishing protocols for access, collection, storage, and retention of ALPR data and associated media files.
3. Closely safeguarding ALPR data using both procedural and technological means.
4

Establishing protocols to preserve and document ALPR reads and alerts that are acted on in the field or
associated with investigations or prosecutions.

Automated License Plate Readers

|. INTRODUCTION

A. Purpose of Document

This paper is designed to accompany the Model Policy on Automated License Plate Readers published by the
IACP Center for Police Research and Policy. This paper provides essential background material and supporting
documentation to provide greater understanding of the developmental philosophy and implementation requirements
for the model policy. It is anticipated that this material will be of value to police executives in their efforts to tailor an
effective automated license plate reader (ALPR) policy to meet their respective agency’s strategic objectives and
operational requirements.

B. Background

A fundamental element of policing is locating vehicles of interest in support of policing’s public safety mission.
To do this, traditionally, officers have worked from vehicle descriptions and license plate lists provided at shift start or
gathered during patrol. This manual system of lists and visual observation is both inefficient and time-consuming.

ALPR systems play an increasingly important role in public safety by enhancing productivity, effectiveness, and
officer safety. ALPR systems can recognize, read, and compare motor vehicle license plates against various “hot lists”
much more efficiently than officers manually scanning and making comparisons while on patrol. ALPR systems can
observe and record over 1,000 license plates an hour in varied lighting and weather conditions. ALPR systems notify
an officer when a license plate on the hot list—a list of license plate numbers identified as being of interest to police—
is read in real time; this can be the case for both fixed and mobile ALPR units. Historical ALPR data can also be
searched to determine the date, time, and location a license plate number was observed by a certain camera.

It is an important distinction that ALPR systems are used to identify vehicles, not persons. In cases where agency
hot lists include license plate numbers of vehicle(s) registered to persons of interest, the ALPR system will alert the
officer to the presence of the vehicle.

Il. How ALPRs FUNCTION

ALPR systems consist of high-speed cameras that capture multiple vehicle images per second. These images are
analyzed by computer algorithms capable of converting the images into electronically readable data and then checked
against hot lists and databases linked to the system.

A. ALPR Operations

ALPR cameras take digital and infrared pictures of vehicles and license plates as they pass through the field of
view of an ALPR camera. These images, and the metadata associated with them (described in more detail below), can

Automated License Plate Readers Concepts and Issues

be used in a variety of public safety contexts. The camera hardware that captures the image of the vehicle is an
essential element of any ALPR system. Hardware can affect image quality, and the quality of the captured image lays
the foundation for the overall performance of the system. ALPR systems typically utilize specialized cameras
designed to capture license plate and vehicle images. However, there are human and environmental factors that pose
difficulty for license plate imaging cameras. To address these difficulties, many ALPR systems employ various
technologies, including infrared cameras operating in addition to visible light cameras.

Images of vehicles and license plates are the primary form of information collected by an ALPR system. Images
captured by ALPR cameras are analyzed through the use of algorithms, including but not limited to functions such as:
e Plate localization, which finds and isolates the license plate contained in the image;

e Plate orientation and sizing, which compensates for the skew of the plate and adjusts the dimensions to
the appropriate size and shape;

e Normalization, which adjusts the brightness and contrast of the image;
e Character segmentation, which finds the individual characters on the plates;

e Optical character recognition (OCR), which converts the image into electronically readable textual
characters; and

e Syntactical/geometrical analysis, which checks characters and positions against state-specific rules to
identify the state of issuance for the license plate.

ALPR cameras can attach metadata such as date, time, and geographic location information to an image. ALPR
systems may contain information including the following:

e OCR of license plate characters;

e Digital images of license plates as well as the vehicle’s make, model, color, and other distinguishing
features (e.g., bumper stickers, damage);
e Digital images of the vehicle’s driver and passengers;
e State of registration;
e Camera identification (identifies which camera captured the image);
e Date and time of image capture; and
e Location of the image capture.
The ALPR captured image provides a more inclusive view of the vehicle and its surroundings. Although a
captured image contained in an ALPR system may contain a great deal of raw information, only certain pieces of

information contained in any ALPR photograph will be subjected to OCR and rendered into an electronically readable
format.

As the technology for ALPR systems advances, the systems themselves may advance with it. For example,
developments in artificial intelligence (AI) should require an in-depth discussion of access to ALPR data from
multiple sources, whether public or private. AI will increase capabilities to associate plates with locations, dates, and
individuals in an investigation. Agencies using AI should ensure that policies are put in place to help ensure the ethical
use of AI within their systems.”

B. ALPR Hot Lists

The primary use of ALPR data involves the comparison of license plate characters collected by an ALPR system
to characters contained on a previously compiled hot list. Hot lists may.be compiled by local, state, and/or federal

Intelligence.

police agencies. Hot lists inform police which vehicles are of interest and why, alerting the user when a potential
match is captured by an ALPR camera. This can be done in real time or through historical ALPR data. As items are
added to a hot list, that information can be checked against existing ALPR data that has been retained by the agency.

The use of hot lists is essential to ALPR systems intended to serve public safety purposes. The actions taken by
ALPR users informed of an alert will vary depending on agency policy, jurisdictional law, and situational context.
Local agencies are ultimately responsible for selecting which hot lists to upload onto their ALPR systems and should
include only those hot lists that further the police agency’s priorities.

1. Compiling and Managing ALPR Hot Lists

Managing hot lists is key to the success of an ALPR system. While some hot lists focus on identifying a
particular vehicle of interest (e.g., stolen cars), other lists include license plate characters known to be associated
with specific persons of interest (e.g., wanted persons). These hot lists, whether they relate to vehicles or persons
of interest, enhance police agencies’ abilities to investigate crime and provide critical officer safety information.

Police agencies should develop a process that sets forth criteria for hot list development and ongoing
accuracy. Hot lists are typically uploaded onto an ALPR system daily and can be updated by the authoring agency
or a user in the field. Hot list information can come from a variety of federal, state, local, or regional sources,
such as:

e The National Crime Information Center
e Departments of motor vehicles
e Other police agencies.
Hot lists may include information such as:
e Date of entry
e Vehicles of interest
e Vehicles associated with missing or endangered persons
e Vehicles associated with wanted persons
e Stolen vehicles

2. Updating and Sharing Hot Lists

When creating or updating hot lists, police agencies should include supporting documentation regarding why
a particular license plate number is on the specific hot list. Information added to a hot list will be seen only by
those with access to that hot list.

Since hot lists are created to enhance an agency’s ability to investigate crime and provide critical officer
safety information, the contents of hot lists should not be disseminated to the public, subject to applicable laws.

Ill. DATA QUALITY AND OCR ACCURACY

ALPR cameras capture images of vehicles and license plates, and OCR software, utilizing algorithms, translates the
characters on each license plate into an electronically readable format. The image collected by an ALPR camera is
maintained in the system for a determined amount of time (see retention in Section JV.F below), to provide a means of
ensuring that the license plate number was properly converted into an electronically readable format. An ALPR system’s
ability to accurately identify the characters on a license plate depends on the data quality.

Many variables affect OCR accuracy. Although each U.S. state has multiple license plate designs, they should all align
with the License Plate Standard published by the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators.* This practice

will lessen the potential for misreads. When jurisdictions change their license plate formats or issue a new license plate
design, OCR accuracy can be substantially impacted. The model policy specifies that users shall visually verify that the
license plate on the vehicle of interest matches the image captured. Poor image resolution may result from human and
environmental factors. Occasionally, for example, a cover or substance might obscure all or a portion of the license plate
and interfere with accurate OCR.

IV. POLICY DEVELOPMENT AND PROCEDURE

A. System Information

Given the different types of ALPR systems (mobile, portable, and fixed), agencies should describe in their ALPR
policy the system(s) and intended operational use.

B. Procedural Concerns and Requirements

AnALPR system collects and stores data related to vehicle location and movement, which can raise significant
privacy concerns from the public. Depending on where the system is deployed, it may inadvertently reveal sensitive
information about the public, such as visits to places of worship, health care facilities, or political gatherings.
Therefore, consideration should be given to the placement of ALPR systems, especially near locations that the public
may view as sensitive. To address public safety and privacy concerns, police agencies must implement clear policies
for their ALPR programs.

ALPR systems can be implemented in ways that respect privacy concerns through well-defined policies
governing data collection, sharing, analysis, and retention. While ALPR technology enhances an agency’s ability to
observe and track vehicles, strong governance and oversight are essential to ensure that the data is only used for
legitimate public safety purposes.

Policies need to define the purpose, use, and data limitations for ALPRs while allowing for secondary uses as
needed. Agencies should designate a program administrator with authority to oversee the ALPR program. The
administrator should, at a minimum:

e Stay current on case law and legislation;

e Monitor the use of the ALPR system and conduct periodic audits, to ensure adherence to law and policy;
e Manage user accounts and permissions;

e Manage ALPR training;

e Update the ALPR policy as needed; and,

e Manage data-sharing agreements.

ALPR systems are only as good as the data they rely on, and ensuring that hot lists are kept current is critical. The
system administrator should establish criteria to determine which hot lists will be uploaded into the ALPR system and
establish any policy and procedures needed to govern manual entries of license plates into the ALPR system. Entries
should be reviewed periodically to determine whether they should be kept, and only authorized users will be given the
necessary permissions to perform this function. Many systems already include technological controls and erase
manual updates after a certain time period. The agency should establish appropriate expirations for manual entries and
update system settings accordingly.

Verifying the accuracy of the license plate read and the hot list information is essential. Prior to initiation of any
action, the responding officer must visually verify that the vehicle plate characters match the plate characters run by

the ALPR system, including characters of the license plate and the state of issuance, and must verify the status of the
alert, such as is it still an active alert.

C. Security Safeguards

ALPR data is categorized as “for official use only” (FOUO). Agency policy should state that misuse of the
equipment, data, or any associated information will result in appropriate disciplinary action. Ensuring that ALPR data
remains secure is one way for police agencies to build public confidence. Police agencies should employ security
protocols, such as audits and system authorizations, to help maintain ALPR data and system access security.

D. Data Sharing and Dissemination

Agencies should review their existing information-sharing policies to determine whether they adequately and
appropriately cover the sharing of ALPR data and should make any modifications to those policies if necessary.
System audit functions help agencies monitor the dissemination of the ALPR data.

Agencies should ensure that information sharing among external entities is conducted in accordance with
statutory limitations and pre-established data-sharing agreements. This could be in the form of an established
memorandum of understanding (MOU), or other established parameters that outline what can be shared, the purpose
of sharing, any limitations, and responsibilities of all involved. Where no such formal MOU is in place, permission
from the person responsible for administering the ALPR system or the designated agency personnel should be
required. Some agencies may also have software in place to provide outside entities with certain information that can
be searched for and/or viewed. Dissemination of data and information sharing should be logged with details of the
request to include information such as:

1. The requesting entity,

2. The scope and reason for the request,

3. The data provided,

4. The data and time of the request, and

5. The personnel who authorized the request.

E. Acquisition of Data

The ALPR acquisition process is designed to be continuous, collecting data from all vehicles in view of the
camera. In addition to system collection, agencies often obtain access to shared ALPR databases maintained by other
vendors, which distribute plate data from entities such as toll booths, parking facilities, and other authorized sources.
An agency should outline what qualifies as an “authorized source.”

F. Retention and Purging of Data

When developing policy, consideration should be given to the fact that privacy concerns are often framed in the
context of retention.’ Unless established by law, agencies should determine the retention policy put in place. The
following criteria should be considered in establishing retention policies:

e Jurisdictional data retention schedules—Jurisdictional data retention schedules supersede retention
periods established by individual entities. Even where there are no jurisdictional guidelines directly
focused on license plate readers, existing guidelines related to comparable forms of electronic data and
imaging systems may be applicable to ALPR systems. Agencies should keep accurate records of what
data is retained and when it is purged.

e Situational realities—Technical and financial realities are different in every jurisdiction, and each must be
considered based on the priorities of the agency.

° For additional information, see the IACP’s Privacy Impact Assessment Report for the Utilization of License Plate Readers.

e Potential evidentiary value—Potential evidentiary value may affect not only the length of retention but
how the data are retained. While saved ALPR data are no longer subject to the original retention period,
such as when it is associated with an active investigation, they may still be subject to policies regarding
evidentiary practices.

G. Auditing

Effective auditing should include maintaining detailed logs of who accessed data, when, and for what reason,
along with records of data retention and purging. Agencies should conduct audits regularly and use findings to
improve training, update procedures, and take corrective action when misuse is detected. By completing regular

audits, agencies can strengthen public trust, ensure legal compliance, and uphold the integrity of their data acquisition
and retention practices.

V. TRAINING

Effective and responsible implementation of ALPR systems requires initial and recurring training to uphold
operational integrity and ensure legal compliance. Personnel with access to the agency’s ALPR system and data
should be trained in system operation, encompassing both hardware and software components. Training should also
encompass data protection protocols, such as data sharing and dissemination, requiring a nuanced understanding of
legal constraints and technical interagency collaboration. Training should reinforce that ALPR data is not exempt from
privacy rights and is subject to applicable laws. Where interagency data sharing is permitted, training should also
cover any legal requirements that govern data sharing.

Automated license plate readers (ALPRs), including Flock, have become one of the most valuable
investigative tools developed in decades. They routinely help officers locate abducted children, recover
stolen vehicles, identify fleeing suspects, and generate investigative leads that would not otherwise
exist. For many agencies, they have become an indispensable force multiplier.

Despite these benefits, no recent law enforcement technology has generated greater public concern.
The debate is not centered on whether ALPRs work; instead, it focuses on whether the technology
could be misused to monitor the movements of law-abiding citizens. As ALPR networks have expanded
and data sharing has increased, public attention has shifted from the technology's crime-fighting value
to the safeguards that prevent abuse. The constitutional question regarding the legality of ALPRs is
important, but public acceptance ultimately depends on transparency, accountability, and responsible
use.

Why the Public Is Concerned

Most public concerns fall into the following categories: government surveillance, the collection of
information about innocent motorists, long-term retention of location data, sharing among agencies,
and the perception that police can ‘track everyone.’ Although ALPR systems capture only discrete
observations rather than continuous GPS-style tracking, many citizens view historical searches as the
practical equivalent.

Media coverage has amplified these concerns. Highly publicized stories involving officers who allegedly
used ALPR systems to monitor former partners, acquaintances, or family members have reinforced
fears that a valuable investigative tool can also be abused if agencies fail to provide meaningful
oversight.

The Reality: Misuse Has Occurred

The overwhelming majority of officers use ALPR systems professionally and only for legitimate law
enforcement purposes. Every day, lawful searches help solve crimes and protect communities.
However, a relatively small number of misuse cases have received national attention. These incidents
have involved officers allegedly accessing ALPR databases for personal reasons, including stalking,
monitoring former romantic partners, and conducting curiosity searches. Although statistically rare,
these cases have had a disproportionate effect on public confidence because they reinforce concerns
about government surveillance. The lesson for police leaders is clear: public trust depends not only on
constitutional compliance, but also on strong policies, meaningful auditing, and swift accountability.
Officer Misuse

Recent investigations illustrate recurring patterns of misuse. The most common involved officers using
Flock to monitor spouses, former partners, family members, neighbors, or acquaintances. Other cases

involved repeated searches of a single license plate, sharing access with unauthorized users, entering
false justification codes, or using ALPR data for purely personal reasons.

Georgia has experienced several high-profile investigations, including Albany, where five officers were
arrested and terminated following an audit, and Savannah, where multiple employees were fired after
investigators uncovered unauthorized searches and improper data sharing. Similar cases have resulted
in arrests, resignations, or terminations in Wisconsin, South Carolina, Massachusetts, Arizona, Florida,
Texas, North Carolina, Ohio, and California.

Perhaps the most important lesson is how these cases were discovered. Some resulted from victim
complaints, while others were uncovered only after agencies conducted proactive audits. Collectively,
they demonstrate that written policies alone are insufficient unless agencies regularly review search
activity and investigate suspicious patterns.

Why These Incidents Matter

One officer's misconduct can affect every agency using ALPR technology. The public rarely judges the
technology by the millions of legitimate searches performed each year. Instead, it remembers the
handful of abuse cases that become national headlines.

As a result, isolated misconduct influences legislative proposals, public opinion, and confidence in law
enforcement generally. Constitutional compliance may answer whether agencies can use ALPR
technology, but public trust depends on whether citizens believe agencies will use it responsibly. Trust
takes years to build and only one well-publicized misuse case to undermine.

Misuse of law enforcement databases is not new. Officers have long been disciplined for improperly
accessing NCIC, driver's license records, and other criminal justice systems. The difference with ALPR
technology is the type of information available.

Traditional databases generally provide static information. ALPR systems can help reconstruct portions
of a vehicle's travel history, allowing investigators to identify where a vehicle has been over time. That
capability is what makes the technology so valuable, and what makes misuse feel more intrusive to the
public.

When an officer improperly accesses a driver's license record, citizens generally view it as an
unauthorized records inquiry. When an officer improperly reconstructs another person's movements,
many perceive it as stalking. That distinction explains why ALPR misuse often generates far greater
public concern than similar misuse of traditional law enforcement databases.

For police leaders, the lesson is straightforward. The more powerful the investigative tool, the greater
the responsibility to ensure it is used only for legitimate law enforcement purposes through sound policy,
active supervision, routine audits, and meaningful accountability.

The Road Ahead

The issues discussed in this article are only the beginning of a much larger constitutional and
operational conversation. As ALPR technology becomes more sophisticated and more widely
deployed, law enforcement agencies must understand not only what the technology can do, but also
the legal principles that govern its use.

The remaining articles in this series examine those issues in detail. Article Two reviews the United
States Supreme Court decisions that form the constitutional framework for evaluating ALPR technology
under the Fourth Amendment. Article Three examines how lower federal and state courts have applied
those principles to ALPR and Flock database searches, explaining why most courts have concluded
that accessing historical ALPR data does not constitute a Fourth Amendment search. Article Four shifts
from database searches to traffic stops, analyzing when an ALPR or Flock alert provides reasonable
suspicion to justify stopping a vehicle and identifying the legal principles officers should apply before

As discussed in Part One of this series, automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) such at Flock have
played a significant role in helping law enforcement officers solve crimes. This article will first examine
precedent from the Supreme Court of the United States that support the legality of the use of such
systems and, second, will examine circumstances that could jeopardize the legal of these systems.

Defining a Reasonable Expectation of Privacy

Although the Supreme Court has never directly addressed the constitutionality of automated license
plate reader (ALPR) systems such as Flock, its Fourth Amendment decisions establish the
constitutional framework for analyzing them. Those decisions answer several important questions that
ultimately determine whether the use of ALPR technology constitutes a Fourth Amendment search.
Specifically, the Court has considered whether individuals have a reasonable expectation of privacy in
information exposed to public view, in information disclosed to third parties, and in their movements on
public roadways. More recently, it has examined when advancing technology transforms ordinary
observations into constitutionally protected surveillance.

Katz v. United States: The Reasonable Expectation of Privacy

The starting point for every Fourth Amendment analysis is Katz v. United States.' There, FBI agents
placed an electronic listening device on the outside of a public telephone booth and recorded the
defendant's telephone conversations without first obtaining a warrant. Although the agents never
entered the booth, the Supreme Court concluded that the government's conduct violated the Fourth
Amendment.

Justice Harlan's concurring opinion, which later became the governing Fourth Amendment test,
explained that constitutional protection depends upon whether a person has (1) exhibited a subjective
expectation of privacy and (2) whether that expectation is one society is prepared to recognize as
reasonable.

Constitutional Principle: The Fourth Amendment protects people—not simply places. Whether
government conduct constitutes a search generally depends upon whether it intrudes upon a
reasonable expectation of privacy.

1 Katz v. United States, 389 U.S. 347 (1967)

That principle remains an issue for every constitutional challenge involving emerging surveillance
technology, including ALPR systems. The remaining Supreme Court cases simply apply that framework
to different types of information and different investigative technologies.

New York v. Class: There Is No Reasonable Expectation of Privacy in a Vehicle's VIN

Nearly twenty years later, the Supreme Court considered whether officers violated the Fourth
Amendment by moving papers on a vehicle's dashboard in order to view the vehicle identification
number (VIN).2

The Court concluded that no reasonable expectation of privacy existed because federal law requires
the VIN to be displayed in plain view. As the Court explained:

It is unreasonable to have an expectation of privacy in an object required by law to
be located in a place ordinarily in plain view from the exterior of the automobile .>

The Court further noted that the exterior of a vehicle is "thrust into the public eye," and examining it
therefore does not constitute a Fourth Amendment search.4

Constitutional Principle: A motorist has no reasonable expectation of privacy in a VIN or other
identifying information that federal law requires to be displayed in plain view on the exterior of a vehicle.

Although Class involved a VIN rather than a license plate, the reasoning extends naturally to license
plates because both are government-issued identifiers displayed on the exterior of a vehicle for public
observation.

Extending Class to License Plates

Federal appellate courts have consistently applied the reasoning of Class to license plates. One of the
leading decisions is United States v. Miranda-Sotolongo, where the Seventh Circuit held that an officer's
use of a license plate number to access a state's vehicle registration database is not a Fourth
Amendment search.§

Rather than viewing the database inquiry as an intrusion upon privacy, the court emphasized that

Public Travel and Technological Surveillance

The next series of Supreme Court decisions examines a different aspect of the Fourth Amendment.
Rather than asking whether individuals have a reasonable expectation of privacy in information
exposed to public view, these cases address whether people have a reasonable expectation of privacy
in their movements while traveling on public roadways. As technology evolved from visual
surveillance to GPS tracking and historical location data, the Court was required to determine whether
traditional constitutional principles remained adequate in the face of increasingly sophisticated
surveillance capabilities.

United States v. Knotts: There ls No Reasonable Expectation of Privacy in Public Travel

The Supreme Court first addressed this issue in United States v. Knotts.’ Investigators suspected
several individuals of manufacturing illegal drugs and secretly placed a radio "beeper" inside a container
of chemicals purchased by one of the suspects. Officers then used the beeper, together with visual
surveillance, to follow the vehicle carrying the container over public roadways to a secluded cabin where
the drugs were ultimately discovered.

The defendants argued that the electronic monitoring constituted a Fourth Amendment search because
it allowed officers to track the vehicle's movements without a warrant. The Supreme Court disagreed.

concurring Justices focused on a different concern that would later prove significant in Carpenter.

pervasive that traditional Fourth Amendment analysis becomes more complicated.

That concern reached its fullest expression six years later in Carpenter v. United States, where the
Supreme Court directly confronted the constitutional implications of long-term historical location

When Technology Crosses the Constitutional Line

The decisions discussed thus far establish two important constitutional principles. First, individuals
generally have no reasonable expectation of privacy in information knowingly exposed to public view,
such as a vehicle's license plate or VIN. Second, motorists ordinarily have no reasonable expectation
of privacy in their movements on public roadways because those movements are visible to anyone who
chooses to observe them.

Carpenter v. United States required the Supreme Court to determine whether those traditional
principles remained adequate in an era when advancing technology could record, store, and
reconstruct virtually every movement a person makes over an extended period of time.

Carpenter v. United States: Comprehensive Historical Location Tracking

Carpenter arose from a series of armed robberies in which federal investigators obtained 127 days of
historical cell-site location information (CSLI) from the defendant's cellular service providers without
first obtaining a search warrant. By examining which cell towers the defendant's phone connected to
over time, investigators reconstructed his movements and placed him near the locations of several
robberies. "4

The government argued that no warrant was required because the records belonged to the cellular
providers rather than to the defendant. Relying upon the Court's earlier decisions in United States v.

overrule Knotts, Class, Miller, or Smith. Nor did it establish that every use of technology to assist law
